match.reason: The bank card is a broader right-angled trigonometry card covering all three ratios and finding sides, and its angle example uses sin⁻¹ with a given ratio rather than finding a ratio from two sides and applying tan⁻¹, so it is close but not the same point.

draft.title: Finding an angle with trigonometry
card: Label the sides of the right-angled triangle from the angle you want. Opposite is across from it, adjacent is next to it, and the hypotenuse is the longest side.
Pick the ratio that uses your two known sides: sin = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan = opposite ÷ adjacent. Divide to get a number.
Then use the inverse function on a calculator (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹) to turn that number into the angle. Use the one that matches the ratio you chose.
Example: opposite = 3 and adjacent = 4. tan θ = 3/4 = 0.75, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.75) ≈ 36.9°.
draft.remember: Divide the two known sides, then use the matching inverse function to get the angle.

a.q: A 10 m ladder leans on a wall and reaches 5 m up. What is the angle between the ladder and the ground?
a.why: The wall height is opposite the angle and the ladder is the hypotenuse. sin θ = 5/10 = 0.5, so θ = sin⁻¹(0.5) = 30°. Using tan⁻¹(0.5) gives 26.6°, which uses a ratio that does not match the two known sides.
a.clue: Which two sides do you know, relative to the angle at the ground?

b.q: A wheelchair ramp in Hobart rises 1.2 m over a flat distance of 5 m. What is its angle of slope, to one decimal place?
b.why: The rise is opposite the angle and the flat distance is adjacent. tan θ = 1.2/5 = 0.24, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.24) ≈ 13.5°. Using sin⁻¹(0.24) gives 13.9°, but the 5 m is not the hypotenuse.
b.clue: The rise and the flat distance are opposite and adjacent.

problems.detail: The card re-teaches side labelling and the three ratio definitions (sin = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, and so on). These belong to point 1, The trigonometric ratios. This point should only mention them, not define them again.

A ramp rising 1.2 m over 5 m (about 1:4, roughly 13.5°) is far steeper than Australian access standards allow for wheelchair ramps (AS 1428.1, max 1:14). Calling it a wheelchair ramp gives students a misleading picture. Use a generic ramp or a driveway instead.

check.summary: Both answers check out: 30° for the ladder and 13.5° for the ramp. The card re-defines the ratios from point 1, and the 'wheelchair ramp' in question b is unrealistically steep for Australian standards.

proposal.title: Finding an angle with trigonometry
card: When you know two sides of a right-angled triangle, you can find an angle. Start by naming the two known sides from the angle you want: opposite, adjacent or hypotenuse.
Choose sin, cos or tan, whichever ratio uses both of your known sides. Divide one side by the other to get a number.
Then use the inverse function on a calculator (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹) to turn that number into the angle. It must match the ratio you chose.
Example: opposite = 3 and adjacent = 4, so use tan. tan θ = 3/4 = 0.75, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.75) ≈ 36.9°.
proposal.remember: Divide the two known sides, then use the matching inverse function to get the angle.
